SS0101.name: Juba
SS0101.livelihoods: Mainly crop farming (sorghum) with minor livestock; a cereal-deficit zone with one rainy season, using forest and wild foods and bush products for food and income.
SS0101.history: Multi-ethnic county hosting Juba, the national capital and county seat; host communities include the Bari, Lokoya and Lulubo; payams include Rejaf, Gondokoro, Mangalla, Lobonok and Wonduruba.
SS0101.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported hostilities between the national army (SSPDF) and the National Salvation Front (NAS) that affected civilians in Juba County in 2023 and 2024, as well as armed incursions by Murle groups near Gondokoro and Mangalla in 2023. According to ACLED, Juba has recorded more political-violence events than any other county since 2018, with deaths among the highest in the country, peaking in 2023, and civilians frequently targeted. The county hosts one of the largest displaced populations in South Sudan, which peaked in 2024, and communal clashes and floods have each displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020. Juba has also become a major destination for people fleeing Sudan's war since 2023. Food insecurity is lower than in most counties, though about half of residents still faced crisis-level hunger or worse in 2024 and 2025.

SS0102.name: Kajo-keji
SS0102.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the bimodal-rainfall Greenbelt, normally a surplus area: maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava, beans; supplemented by small livestock, fishing, hunting and wild/bush products, with cross-border trade.
SS0102.history: Home mainly to the Kuku; borders Uganda. Once seen as a stable model county, it was heavily depopulated by conflict from 2016.
SS0102.conflict_impact: UNMISS found Kajo-Keji, together with Yei, to be among the areas most affected by violence between government forces and the National Salvation Front (NAS) in 2018-19, and fighting between the two again affected parts of the county in 2024. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence compared with other counties, with deaths reaching their highest level in 2025. Displacement peaked in 2018 at the height of that conflict, and communal violence has since displaced tens of thousands more. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger or worse at the 2018 peak; conditions have eased somewhat but remain serious for a large minority.

SS0103.name: Lainya
SS0103.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the bimodal-rainfall Greenbelt, normally a surplus area: maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava, beans; supplemented by small livestock, fishing, hunting and wild/bush products, with cross-border trade.
SS0103.history: County on the Juba-Yei road with headquarters at Lainya town; part of the former Yei River State. Affected by the National Salvation Front (NAS) insurgency since 2016-17.
SS0103.conflict_impact: Villages in Lainya and neighbouring Yei, including Mukaya, were attacked repeatedly in 2018-19, and UNMISS attributed many abductions in Mukaya payam in 2022 to the National Salvation Front (NAS). ACLED records relatively high levels of political violence for the county, with deaths peaking in 2019. The displaced population was relatively large, peaking in 2021, and communal clashes have forced thousands more from their homes. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger or worse at the 2018 peak; the share has since fallen but remains substantial.

SS0104.name: Morobo
SS0104.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the bimodal-rainfall Greenbelt, normally a surplus area: maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava, beans; supplemented by small livestock, fishing, hunting and wild/bush products, with cross-border trade.
SS0104.history: Greenbelt county bordering Uganda and DR Congo, inhabited mainly by Kakwa, Keliko and Lugbara farmers; a food supplier for Yei and Juba.
SS0104.conflict_impact: UNMISS documented abductions by the National Salvation Front (NAS) in Morobo in 2022-23 and, in 2025, aerial bombardment by the national army (SSPDF) of SPLA-IO positions, including the Kendila cantonment site. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths at their highest in 2025. Displacement peaked in 2022, and fighting between armed forces has displaced thousands of people since 2020. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and a large minority still did in 2025.

SS0105.name: Terekeka
SS0105.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum, groundnuts and other crops combined with cattle, goats and sheep; moderately productive, with acute dry-season water shortages and seasonal cattle raiding.
SS0105.history: Mundari agro-pastoralist county on both banks of the White Nile north of Juba, carved out of Juba County in 2001; headquarters Terekeka town.
SS0105.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported intercommunal violence by community-based militias around Juba and Terekeka counties in 2022. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2018. Flooding has been the county's biggest driver of displacement: Terekeka is among the counties where floods have displaced the most people since 2020, while communal clashes displaced thousands more. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and a large minority still did in 2025.

SS0106.name: Yei
SS0106.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the bimodal-rainfall Greenbelt, normally a surplus area: maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava, beans; supplemented by small livestock, fishing, hunting and wild/bush products, with cross-border trade.
SS0106.history: Yei River County, home to Pojulu, Kakwa, Keliko, Makaraka, Mundu and others; Yei town is a cross-border trade hub near Uganda and DR Congo and hosts IDPs and Congolese refugees.
SS0106.conflict_impact: Yei was the epicentre of the 2018-19 conflict between government forces and the National Salvation Front (NAS) documented by UNMISS, and NAS abductions in Lasu, Otogo and Tore payams continued from 2022 to 2025. ACLED records one of the highest numbers of political-violence events of any county, with deaths at their worst in 2018. The county has had a relatively large displaced population, peaking in 2021. Hunger has been less severe than in most of the country, and the share of people in crisis has fallen since 2019.

SS0201.name: Budi
SS0201.livelihoods: Mainly crop farming (sorghum) with minor livestock; a cereal-deficit zone with one rainy season, using forest and wild foods and bush products for food and income.
SS0201.history: Named after its Buya and Didinga agro-pastoralist inhabitants; headquarters Chukudum, which hosted the first SPLM National Convention in 1994. Borders Uganda and Kenya.
SS0201.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported a 2024 attack on Didinga honey harvesters in Budi's mountains, an area contested with Karamojong communities from Uganda. ACLED records relatively high levels of political violence for the county, much of it directed at civilians, with deaths peaking in 2021. Displacement has been comparatively limited. Hunger was severe at its 2019 peak, when most residents faced crisis-level food insecurity or worse, but has eased considerably since.

SS0202.name: Ikotos
SS0202.livelihoods: Mainly crop farming (sorghum) with minor livestock; a cereal-deficit zone with one rainy season, using forest and wild foods and bush products for food and income. Also partly in the Equatorial maize and cassava zone.
SS0202.history: Highland county around Ikotos town inhabited by Lango, Ketebo and other agro-pastoral groups growing sorghum and millet; dry-season cattle raiding has long occurred, notably in the Kidepo valley.
SS0202.conflict_impact: UNMISS documented incursions in 2024 by armed Logir elements in Chokorol payam, Ikotos, which killed and injured civilians. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2022. Communal clashes have displaced thousands of people since 2020. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2019 peak, but food security has improved markedly since.

SS0203.name: Kapoeta East
SS0203.livelihoods: Pastoralism (cattle, goats, sheep) with very limited cropping in a semi-arid zone; wild foods and market purchase, including grain from Kenya and Ethiopia, fill the food gap.
SS0203.history: Largest group is the Toposa pastoralists, with the Jie minority in Jie payam and Nyangatom near the Kenya-Ethiopia border; payams include Narus, Natinga and Kauto.
SS0203.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported cross-border attacks on Toposa communities by armed Turkana from Kenya in 2023, and armed Murle raids from the Greater Pibor Administrative Area in 2024-25. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths rising to their highest level in 2024. Communal violence has displaced thousands of people since 2020. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2019 peak; the share has since fallen but remains significant.

SS0204.name: Kapoeta North
SS0204.livelihoods: Pastoralism (cattle, goats, sheep) with very limited cropping in a semi-arid zone; wild foods and market purchase, including grain from Kenya and Ethiopia, fill the food gap.
SS0204.history: Toposa pastoralist county whose principal settlement is Riwoto.
SS0204.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported Murle armed elements from the Greater Pibor Administrative Area reaching parts of Kapoeta North in 2024. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2022. Displacement has been relatively limited compared with other counties. Hunger was severe at its 2019 peak, affecting most residents, and has since eased, though a large minority still face crisis conditions.

SS0205.name: Kapoeta South
SS0205.livelihoods: Pastoralism (cattle, goats, sheep) with very limited cropping in a semi-arid zone; wild foods and market purchase, including grain from Kenya and Ethiopia, fill the food gap.
SS0205.history: Toposa and Didinga county around Kapoeta town (county HQ), with Kapoeta Mission Hospital serving a large catchment including returnees and IDPs.
SS0205.conflict_impact: According to ACLED, Kapoeta South has seen relatively little political violence compared with other counties, though deaths rose to their highest level in 2024. Displacement has been limited, peaking in 2019. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2019 peak; conditions have since improved, though a significant minority remain in crisis.

SS0206.name: Lafon
SS0206.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: rain-fed sorghum plus cattle herding on floodplains, supplemented by fishing, hunting and wild foods; a cereal-deficit area rich in fish and livestock products. Also partly in the South-Eastern semi-arid pastoral zone.
SS0206.history: Also called Lopa/Lafon; largest community is the Lopit, followed by the Pari, Tennet and Lotuko; mostly single-season farmers.
SS0206.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported raids by Murle armed elements from the Greater Pibor Administrative Area on Pari and Toposa communities in Lafon between 2023 and 2025. ACLED records relatively little political violence overall, with deaths peaking in 2023. Displacement has continued to grow, reaching its highest level in early 2025, and floods have displaced thousands. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2023 peak, and close to half still did in 2025.

SS0207.name: Magwi
SS0207.livelihoods: Mainly crop farming (sorghum) with minor livestock; a cereal-deficit zone with one rainy season, using forest and wild foods and bush products for food and income.
SS0207.history: Acholi county bordering Uganda; towns include Magwi (headquarters), Nimule, Pageri, Palotaka and Pajok, with the White Nile entering at Nimule.
SS0207.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported intercommunal violence involving Dinka Bor cattle keepers in and around Magwi County in the first half of 2022. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest that same year. Displacement also peaked in 2022 and was relatively high, with communal clashes alone displacing tens of thousands of people since 2020. Hunger has been less severe than in most counties and has eased further since 2019.

SS0208.name: Torit
SS0208.livelihoods: Mainly crop farming (sorghum) with minor livestock; a cereal-deficit zone with one rainy season, using forest and wild foods and bush products for food and income.
SS0208.history: Seat of Torit town, capital of Eastern Equatoria; inhabited by Lotuko (Otuho), Madi and Acholi groups; affected by the Second Sudanese Civil War and LRA activity.
SS0208.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported Murle armed elements from the Greater Pibor Administrative Area reaching parts of Torit County in 2023-24. ACLED records a relatively high number of political-violence events, with deaths peaking in 2022. Internal displacement has been among the lowest of any county, though Torit has received some people fleeing Sudan's war. Food insecurity is lower than in much of the country: about half of residents were in crisis at the 2019 peak, and fewer are today.

SS0301.name: Akobo
SS0301.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: rain-fed sorghum plus cattle herding on floodplains, supplemented by fishing, hunting and wild foods; a cereal-deficit area rich in fish and livestock products.
SS0301.history: Lou Nuer county on the Ethiopian border with headquarters at Akobo town; a pastoral population that moves with livestock in search of water and pasture, and some residents have sought refuge in Ethiopia.
SS0301.conflict_impact: UNMISS documented recurring cycles of attack and cattle raiding between Lou Nuer and Murle communities affecting Akobo in 2020 and again from 2022 to 2024. ACLED records relatively high levels of political violence, with civilians frequently targeted and deaths peaking in 2023. Floods and armed conflict have each displaced thousands of people since 2020. Hunger has been severe: the vast majority of residents faced crisis-level food insecurity or worse at the 2022 peak, and more than half still did in 2025.

SS0302.name: Ayod
SS0302.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: rain-fed sorghum plus cattle herding on floodplains, supplemented by fishing, hunting and wild foods; a cereal-deficit area rich in fish and livestock products. Also partly in the Nile basin fishing and agro-pastoral zone.
SS0302.history: Inhabited by the Gawaar (Gaawar) Nuer; part of the Sudd-edge floodplain of northern Jonglei.
SS0302.conflict_impact: According to UNMISS, the Gawaar Nuer 'White Army' militia from Ayod fought alongside the Kitgwang faction in Upper Nile between August and December 2022. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths rising to their highest level in 2025. Flooding is a major driver of displacement: Ayod is among the counties where floods have forced the most people from their homes since 2020, and armed conflict has displaced thousands more. The vast majority of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2022 peak; conditions have since eased but remain serious for nearly half.

SS0303.name: Bor South
SS0303.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: rain-fed sorghum plus cattle herding on floodplains, supplemented by fishing, hunting and wild foods; a cereal-deficit area rich in fish and livestock products.
SS0303.history: Dinka Bor county containing Bor town, the capital of Jonglei State, on the east bank of the White Nile.
SS0303.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported armed Murle raids into Bor South in 2020 and 2023-24, and the involvement of Dinka Bor cattle keepers in violence around Magwi in 2022. ACLED records relatively high levels of political violence, with deaths peaking in 2020. The county has one of the largest displaced populations in the country, peaking in 2023, and communal violence and floods have each displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, but conditions have improved substantially since.

SS0304.name: Canal/Pigi
SS0304.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: rain-fed sorghum plus cattle herding on floodplains, supplemented by fishing, hunting and wild foods; a cereal-deficit area rich in fish and livestock products.
SS0304.history: Northwestern Jonglei county on the White Nile corridor, home to Padang Dinka (Paweny, Thoi, Rut, Luac), Gawaar and Lou Nuer, and Shilluk communities.
SS0304.conflict_impact: According to UNMISS, armed elements from Pigi joined the 2022 fighting in Upper Nile, and Pigi and neighbouring Fangak were hit by violence spilling over from Upper Nile in 2025. ACLED records relatively few deaths overall, but they reached their highest level in 2025. The county has one of the largest displaced populations in the country, which peaked in 2023, and floods have displaced thousands more. Hunger here is among the most severe in South Sudan: the vast majority of residents faced crisis-level food insecurity or worse at the 2019 peak, and most still did in 2025.

SS0305.name: Duk
SS0305.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: rain-fed sorghum plus cattle herding on floodplains, supplemented by fishing, hunting and wild foods; a cereal-deficit area rich in fish and livestock products. Also partly in the Nile basin fishing and agro-pastoral zone.
SS0305.history: Primarily Dinka county (per UNMISS) south of the Sudd; Duk Payuel is the birthplace of 'Lost Boy' John Dau.
SS0305.conflict_impact: UNMISS documented recurring armed Murle attacks on Duk in 2020 and 2023, and in 2024 the county accounted for a disproportionate share of Jonglei's civilian victims of such violence. ACLED records relatively high levels of political violence, with civilians frequently targeted and deaths peaking in 2024. Displacement rose to its highest level in early 2025, and floods have displaced thousands. The vast majority of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak; the share has since fallen, though a large minority remain in crisis.

SS0306.name: Fangak
SS0306.livelihoods: Riverine livelihoods along the Nile/Sudd: fishing combined with sorghum and maize cropping and cattle, goats and sheep, plus water lilies and other wild foods; floods recur every few years. Also partly in the Eastern plains sorghum and cattle zone.
SS0306.history: Inhabited mainly by the Laak and Thiang sections of the Nuer, agro-pastoralists of the Sudd; headquarters Phom el Zeraf where the Bahr el Zeraf meets the White Nile.
SS0306.conflict_impact: OCHA identified Fangak as the most flood-affected county in South Sudan in 2021; fighting reached New Fangak in 2022, and air strikes on Old Fangak in May 2025 killed civilians. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence overall, with deaths highest in 2025. According to IOM displacement tracking, floods and armed conflict have each displaced more people in Fangak than in any other county since 2020, its displaced population was among the largest in the country in 2024, and it has also received many people fleeing Sudan's war. Hunger is among the most severe in South Sudan: the vast majority of residents faced crisis-level food insecurity or worse at the 2022 peak, and nearly as many still did in 2025.

SS0307.name: Nyirol
SS0307.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: rain-fed sorghum plus cattle herding on floodplains, supplemented by fishing, hunting and wild foods; a cereal-deficit area rich in fish and livestock products.
SS0307.history: Lou Nuer county (per UNMISS) in northern Jonglei; Lankien is a main town.
SS0307.conflict_impact: UNMISS documented Murle raids on Nyirol in 2020 and 2023-24, and a 2022 attack in Fashoda carried out by Lou Nuer youth from Lankien. ACLED records relatively high levels of political violence, with civilians frequently targeted and deaths peaking in 2024. Communal clashes and wider armed conflict have each displaced thousands of people since 2020, with the displaced population peaking in 2023. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2019 peak, and more than half still did in 2025.

SS0308.name: Pibor
SS0308.livelihoods: Pastoralism (cattle, goats, sheep) with very limited cropping in a semi-arid zone; wild foods and market purchase, including grain from Kenya and Ethiopia, fill the food gap.
SS0308.history: Home of the Murle, Kachipo and Jie; seat of the Greater Pibor Administrative Area (GPAA), announced in 2020; headquarters Pibor town. Areas include Gumuruk, Likuangole and Verteth.
SS0308.conflict_impact: Dinka and Nuer militias attacked Likuangole and Gumuruk in 2020, and Nuer militias launched a large attack on the Greater Pibor Administrative Area on 24 December 2022, according to UNMISS. ACLED data place Pibor among the deadliest counties in South Sudan, with deaths peaking in 2022. Communal violence and floods have each displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020. Hunger is among the most severe in the country: the vast majority of residents faced crisis-level food insecurity or worse at the 2022 peak, and most still did in 2025.

SS0309.name: Pochalla

livelihood_zone.name: Maize Sorghum Fishing and Natural Resources

SS0309.livelihoods: Farming (maize, sorghum) with two harvests, supplemented by livestock, fishing and natural resources such as honey and shea from the Boma/Badingilo area.
SS0309.history: Anyuak (Anuak) farming county on the Ethiopian border, part of the Greater Pibor Administrative Area; hosts Ethiopian Anyuak refugees.
SS0309.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported incursions by Murle armed elements into parts of Pochalla in 2024. ACLED records relatively little political violence compared with other counties, with deaths highest in 2023. Floods and armed conflict have each displaced thousands of people, and displacement peaked in 2024. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2023 peak, and about half still did in 2025.

SS0310.name: Twic East
SS0310.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: rain-fed sorghum plus cattle herding on floodplains, supplemented by fishing, hunting and wild foods; a cereal-deficit area rich in fish and livestock products. Also partly in the Nile basin fishing and agro-pastoral zone.
SS0310.history: Twic (Twi) Dinka county with headquarters at Panyagor; former Twi Dinka district in colonial times and birthplace of John Garang.
SS0310.conflict_impact: UNMISS documented Murle raids into Twic East in 2020 and 2024. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2025. Floods have displaced thousands of people since 2020, and displacement peaked in 2024. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2022 peak, and about half still did in 2025.

SS0311.name: Uror
SS0311.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: rain-fed sorghum plus cattle herding on floodplains, supplemented by fishing, hunting and wild foods; a cereal-deficit area rich in fish and livestock products.
SS0311.history: Lou Nuer county in northern Jonglei; home area of Gen. Simon Gatwech Dual, former SPLA-IO chief of staff.
SS0311.conflict_impact: UNMISS documented Murle raids on Uror in 2020 and 2023, part of wider cycles of violence between Lou Nuer and Murle communities. ACLED places Uror among the deadliest counties in the country, with deaths peaking in 2020. Floods, communal clashes and wider armed conflict have together displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2022 peak, and more than half still did in 2025.

SS0401.name: Awerial
SS0401.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum, groundnuts and other crops combined with cattle, goats and sheep; moderately productive, with acute dry-season water shortages and seasonal cattle raiding. Also partly in the Nile basin fishing and agro-pastoral zone.
SS0401.history: Aliab Dinka county with headquarters at Mingkaman on the White Nile. Mingkaman received tens of thousands of IDPs from Bor South, Twic East and Duk by Jan 2014; little direct 2013-18 fighting.
SS0401.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that reciprocal raiding between Aliab Dinka and Mundari communities near the Terekeka border rose in 2020-21, and that severe Nile flooding in mid-2020 displaced riverside settlements. ACLED records relatively little political violence compared with other counties, with deaths highest in 2020. Awerial has hosted one of the largest displaced populations in the country, peaking in 2019, reflecting Mingkaman's role since 2014 as a refuge for people fleeing fighting in Jonglei; floods have displaced tens of thousands more. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and the share has since fallen substantially.

SS0402.name: Cueibet
SS0402.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum, groundnuts and other crops combined with cattle, goats and sheep; moderately productive, with acute dry-season water shortages and seasonal cattle raiding.
SS0402.history: Gok Dinka county with headquarters at Cueibet town; relatively insulated from the 1983-2005 and 2013-2018 wars but affected by intra-Gok sectional conflict since the late 1990s.
SS0402.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that inter-sectional raiding rose after the 2018 peace agreement (R-ARCSS), with cross-border violence involving Agar Dinka in 2021 and Tonj South in late 2022, before easing from 2022. ACLED places Cueibet among the deadliest counties in the country, with deaths peaking in 2021. Displacement has been comparatively limited. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, but food security has improved markedly since.

SS0403.name: Rumbek Centre

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0403.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum (staple), maize and groundnuts with cattle, goats and sheep (most households own cattle), plus fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit, trading livestock for grain.
SS0403.history: Agar Dinka county containing Rumbek, capital of Lakes State and SPLM/A headquarters after 1997; not directly affected by SPLA vs SPLA-IO fighting in 2013-2018.
SS0403.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that after 2018, clashes among Agar Dinka sections and with Gok Dinka grew more lethal, and that a new state governor imposed coercive security measures from 2021. ACLED records relatively high levels of political violence, with deaths peaking in 2021. Displacement within the county has been among the lowest in the country. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and about half still did in 2025.

SS0404.name: Rumbek East

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0404.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum (staple), maize and groundnuts with cattle, goats and sheep (most households own cattle), plus fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit, trading livestock for grain. Also partly in the Ironstone Plateau agro-pastoral zone.
SS0404.history: Agar Dinka county with headquarters in Aduel payam; long affected by inter- and intra-sectional feuds and cattle raiding from southern Unity State.
SS0404.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that fighting between the Gony and Thuyic sub-sections escalated in 2019-2021 despite a November 2019 peace deal, and that cross-border violence with Yirol West also flared. ACLED records relatively high levels of political violence, with deaths peaking in 2021. Displacement has been comparatively limited. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak; the share has since fallen to under half.

SS0405.name: Rumbek North

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0405.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum (staple), maize and groundnuts with cattle, goats and sheep (most households own cattle), plus fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit, trading livestock for grain.
SS0405.history: Pakam (Agar) Dinka county at the Lakes-Warrap-Unity tri-border, exposed to disputes over water, grazing and cattle raiding.
SS0405.conflict_impact: Fighting between the Gak and Manuer sections killed dozens of people in November 2019, and clashes between Pakam and Luach-Jang communities on the Tonj East border caused heavy loss of life in February and April 2023 (CSRF, UN Security Council). ACLED places Rumbek North among the deadliest counties in the country, with deaths peaking in 2023. Displacement was relatively high, peaking in late 2019. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2020 peak, and a large minority still did in 2025.

SS0406.name: Wulu
SS0406.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum, groundnuts and other crops combined with cattle, goats and sheep; moderately productive, with acute dry-season water shortages and seasonal cattle raiding.
SS0406.history: Home to the Belle ('Jur Bel') and Bongo farming and fishing communities; hosted the 2000 Wunlit follow-up peace conference.
SS0406.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that raids on cattle camps continued after 2018, including the killing of Gok Dinka cattle traders in December 2019, and that road security improved from 2022. ACLED records relatively little political violence compared with other counties, with deaths highest in 2021. Displacement has been comparatively limited. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, but food security has improved markedly since.

SS0407.name: Yirol East

secondary.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0407.livelihoods: Riverine livelihoods along the Nile/Sudd: fishing combined with sorghum and maize cropping and cattle, goats and sheep, plus water lilies and other wild foods; floods recur every few years. Also partly in the Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle zone.
SS0407.history: Ciec Dinka (Ador, Lou) and Atuot county in Greater Yirol, an SPLM/A stronghold in the second civil war; includes the Nile port of Shambe.
SS0407.conflict_impact: Raiding from Panyijiar in Unity State is a recurring threat, and in June 2025 UNMISS reported a deadly attack on a boat carrying Nuer civilians in Yirol East. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2025. Floods and communal clashes have displaced thousands of people since 2020. The vast majority of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and about half still did in 2025.

SS0408.name: Yirol West
SS0408.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum, groundnuts and other crops combined with cattle, goats and sheep; moderately productive, with acute dry-season water shortages and seasonal cattle raiding.
SS0408.history: Atuot (Reel, Apak) county around Yirol town and Lake Yirol, part of Greater Yirol; payams include Aluakluak, Geer and Mapuordit.
SS0408.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that clashes between Agar Dinka and Atuot communities rose sharply in 2021 in Aluakluak and Gher payams, alongside a deadly clash within the Atuot community that year. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths peaking in 2021. Communal violence has displaced thousands of people, with displacement peaking that same year. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak; the share has since fallen considerably.

SS0501.name: Aweil Centre

livelihood_zone.name: Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum

secondary.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0501.livelihoods: Subsistence rain-fed farming of groundnuts, sesame and sorghum, supplemented by forest products, seasonal river fishing and sales of poultry, goats and sheep; a former surplus area. Also partly in the Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle zone.
SS0501.history: Home to Luo ('Jur Chol') and Dinka Malual communities, headquarters in Aroyo payam; relatively insulated from both the second civil war raids and 2013-2018 fighting, and hosted IDPs from Wau and Raja.
SS0501.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that recent tensions involve land, water points and disputes between Luo farmers and Fulani pastoralists, addressed through peace conferences in 2021 and 2023. ACLED records very little political violence, among the lowest of any county. Floods have displaced thousands of people since 2020, and the county has received a substantial number of people fleeing Sudan's war since 2023. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2022 peak, and a large minority still did in 2025.

SS0502.name: Aweil East

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0502.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum (staple), maize and groundnuts with cattle, goats and sheep (most households own cattle), plus fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit, trading livestock for grain.
SS0502.history: Most populous Dinka Malual (Abiem) county, headquarters at Mabil (Wanyjok area); heavily affected by murahalin raids during the 1983-2005 war and home to several national leaders.
SS0502.conflict_impact: CSRF describes Aweil East as less directly affected by the 2013-18 war, although SSPM/A rebels were active in 2016-18 and caused some displacement. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2020. Floods are the main driver of displacement, with Aweil East among the counties most affected since 2020, and it is also one of the main destinations for people fleeing Sudan's war since 2023. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2022 peak, and about half still did in 2025.

SS0503.name: Aweil North

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0503.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum (staple), maize and groundnuts with cattle, goats and sheep (most households own cattle), plus fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit, trading livestock for grain.
SS0503.history: Dinka Malual (Giernyang) county with headquarters at Gok Machar, on the disputed border with Sudan incl. the '14-Mile Area'; badly hit by murahalin raids in 1983-2005.
SS0503.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that Aweil North was directly affected early in the 2013-18 war, and that since 2023 the state has hosted people fleeing the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan. ACLED records very little political violence since 2018. Flooding is the dominant cause of displacement, with Aweil North among the counties where floods have displaced the most people since 2020, and it has received a substantial number of arrivals from Sudan. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2020 peak, and about half still did in 2025.

SS0504.name: Aweil South

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0504.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum (staple), maize and groundnuts with cattle, goats and sheep (most households own cattle), plus fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit, trading livestock for grain.
SS0504.history: Dinka Malual (Paliet) and Luo ('Jur Chol') county with headquarters in Nyocawany payam, away from the Sudan border; few direct effects of the 2013-2018 war.
SS0504.conflict_impact: CSRF describes mostly low-level, localised conflict since 2018, such as an April 2019 boundary dispute over Wathmuok among Paliet sub-sections that was resolved at a peace conference. ACLED records very little political violence, among the lowest of any county. Floods have displaced thousands of people since 2020. Hunger has worsened recently: crisis-level food insecurity reached its highest level in 2024, affecting most residents, and more than half were still affected in 2025.

SS0505.name: Aweil West

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0505.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum (staple), maize and groundnuts with cattle, goats and sheep (most households own cattle), plus fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit, trading livestock for grain.
SS0505.history: Dinka Malual and Luo ('Jur Chol') county with headquarters at Nyamlel; Nyamlel and Marial Bai were severely hit by militia raids during the 1983-2005 war.
SS0505.conflict_impact: CSRF reports isolated incidents between Dinka Malual and Rizeigat communities in 2020-21 and land disputes in 2022-24, at levels far below those of the second civil war. ACLED records very little political violence. Even so, the county has had a relatively large displaced population, peaking in 2019; floods have displaced tens of thousands since 2020, and it has received a substantial number of people fleeing Sudan's war. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and a large minority still did in 2025.

SS0601.name: Abiemnhom
SS0601.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism: sorghum and livestock, supplemented by Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade; mechanised farming near the Nile, otherwise subsistence with a cereal deficit.
SS0601.history: Padang Dinka (Alor) county on the contested Sudan border, part of the Ruweng Administrative Area (RAA) established in 2020.
SS0601.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that road ambushes and tensions between Bul Nuer and Alor Dinka communities have dominated since 2018, including a deadly cattle raid in 2022. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2025. Displacement has been comparatively limited. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2022 peak, and a large minority still did in 2025.

SS0602.name: Guit

livelihood_zone.name: North-Western Nile basin cattle and maize

SS0602.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral with stronger focus on cattle than crops; maize is the main staple, with fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit relying on imports from Sudan. Also partly in the Nile basin fishing and agro-pastoral zone.
SS0602.history: Western Jikany Nuer county created in 2005; held mainly by SPLA-IO in 2013-2018 despite government offensives in 2014, 2015 and 2018.
SS0602.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that police officers were killed pursuing raiders from Mayom in May 2021, that clashes between Guit and Pariang communities turned deadly in February 2022, and that the national army (SSPDF) and SPLA-IO fought in December 2023. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2018. Displacement has grown, reaching its highest level in early 2025, and floods have displaced thousands. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2019 peak, and most still did in 2025.

SS0603.name: Koch

livelihood_zone.name: North-Western Nile basin cattle and maize

SS0603.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral with stronger focus on cattle than crops; maize is the main staple, with fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit relying on imports from Sudan.
SS0603.history: Jagey (Jagei) Nuer county in central Unity, a frontline in past wars and site of the Thar Jath oil field.
SS0603.conflict_impact: Fighting around the Mirmir SPLA-IO cantonment site in February-April 2022 was part of the wave of violence in southern Unity in which UNMISS documented large-scale killings of civilians. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2021. Floods have displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020. The vast majority of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and most still did in 2025.

SS0604.name: Leer

secondary.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0604.livelihoods: Riverine livelihoods along the Nile/Sudd: fishing combined with sorghum and maize cropping and cattle, goats and sheep, plus water lilies and other wild foods; floods recur every few years. Also partly in the Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle zone.
SS0604.history: Dok Nuer county; Leer town was an SPLA-IO stronghold and target of government offensives incl. in 2018.
SS0604.conflict_impact: Between February and May 2022, attacks by government forces and allied militias centred on Leer killed and raped large numbers of civilians and displaced tens of thousands across southern Unity, according to UNMISS. ACLED records relatively high levels of political violence, with deaths peaking in 2022, the same year displacement peaked. Communal violence and floods have each displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020. The vast majority of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and about half still did in 2025.

SS0605.name: Mayendit

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0605.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum (staple), maize and groundnuts with cattle, goats and sheep (most households own cattle), plus fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit, trading livestock for grain.
SS0605.history: Haak Nuer county in southern Unity; an SPLA-IO stronghold hit by government offensives in 2014, 2015 and 2018.
SS0605.conflict_impact: Cross-border cattle raids from Tonj in 2019-20 and tensions between government and opposition forces persisted, and UNMISS implicated Mayendit-based militias in the 2022 attacks on Leer. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths peaking in 2022. Floods have displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020, and displacement reached its highest level in early 2025. The vast majority of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2022 peak; the share has since fallen to under half.

SS0606.name: Mayom

livelihood_zone.name: North-Western Nile basin cattle and maize

SS0606.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral with stronger focus on cattle than crops; maize is the main staple, with fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit relying on imports from Sudan.
SS0606.history: Bul Nuer county with headquarters at Mayom town; home of influential commanders such as the late Paulino Matip.
SS0606.conflict_impact: Splits among local elites led to the SSPM/A rebellion, and in July 2022 an attack on Mayom town killed several people, including the county commissioner (CSRF, OHCHR). ACLED places Mayom among the deadliest counties in the country, with many civilians targeted and deaths peaking in 2019. Floods have displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020, displacement reached its highest level in early 2025, and the county has received thousands of people fleeing Sudan's war. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and about half still did in 2025.

SS0607.name: Panyijiar

secondary.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0607.livelihoods: Riverine livelihoods along the Nile/Sudd: fishing combined with sorghum and maize cropping and cattle, goats and sheep, plus water lilies and other wild foods; floods recur every few years. Also partly in the Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle zone.
SS0607.history: Nyuong Nuer county largely within the Sudd wetlands, bordering Lakes State; an opposition stronghold hit by government offensives in 2014-2015.
SS0607.conflict_impact: Cross-border cattle raiding with communities in Lakes State (Rumbek and Yirol) recurred from 2021 to 2025 despite peace deals in 2018, 2022 and September 2024 (CSRF, UNMISS). ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2025. Floods are the main driver of displacement: Panyijiar is among the counties where flooding has displaced the most people since 2020. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2022 peak, and about half still did in 2025.

SS0608.name: Pariang
SS0608.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism: sorghum and livestock, supplemented by Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade; mechanised farming near the Nile, otherwise subsistence with a cereal deficit.
SS0608.history: Padang Dinka (Ruweng/Panaruu, Paweny) county, seat of the Ruweng Administrative Area created in 2020; loyal to the government in 2013-2018. Hosts Nuba Mountains refugees at Ajoung Thok, Pamir and Yida.
SS0608.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that localised insecurity centres on Wunkur payam, including a deadly clash between the national army (SSPDF) and SPLA-IO in July 2023. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2022. The county has received thousands of people fleeing Sudan's war since 2023, in addition to the refugees from Sudan's Nuba Mountains it has long hosted. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2022 peak, and a large minority still did in 2025.

SS0609.name: Rubkona

livelihood_zone.name: North-Western Nile basin cattle and maize

SS0609.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral with stronger focus on cattle than crops; maize is the main staple, with fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit relying on imports from Sudan.
SS0609.history: Leek Nuer county containing Bentiu (Unity State capital) and Rubkona town, centre of the Unity oil fields; its large UNMISS PoC site became an IDP camp in 2021.
SS0609.conflict_impact: Severe floods in 2021-22 surrounded Bentiu, and the town's displacement camp relies on dykes to stay dry (MSF); in March 2022 a group of Misseriya herders was killed in a grazing dispute (UN Security Council). ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2021. Rubkona hosts the largest displaced population of any county, peaking in 2023, and is one of the main destinations for people fleeing Sudan's war; floods have displaced tens of thousands more. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and most still did in 2025.

SS0701.name: Baliet
SS0701.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism: sorghum and livestock, supplemented by Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade; mechanised farming near the Nile, otherwise subsistence with a cereal deficit.
SS0701.history: Padang Dinka (Ngok Lual Yak) county in central Upper Nile, east of Malakal and crossed by the Sobat, with land disputes involving Nuer to the south and Shilluk along the Nile.
SS0701.conflict_impact: ACLED records moderate levels of political violence in Baliet, a large share of it directed at civilians, with deaths rising to their highest level in 2025. Communal clashes have displaced thousands of people since 2020, while overall displacement peaked in 2018. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2019 peak, and more than half still did in 2025, a higher share than in most counties.

SS0702.name: Fashoda
SS0702.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism: sorghum and livestock, supplemented by Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade; mechanised farming near the Nile, otherwise subsistence with a cereal deficit.
SS0702.history: Seen by the Shilluk (Chollo) as the heart of their kingdom; includes Kodok (county seat) and Tonga. Shilluk-Padang Dinka territorial disputes date to the second civil war.
SS0702.conflict_impact: Fighting between the Kitgwang faction and allied White Army militia and Agwelek forces from August to December 2022 hit Tonga and Kodok, and tens of thousands of people sheltered at Kodok near the UNMISS base. ACLED records relatively high levels of political violence, much of it against civilians, with deaths peaking in 2022. Communal violence has displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020, and the county has received a substantial number of people fleeing Sudan's war. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2019 peak, and a large minority still did in 2025.

SS0703.name: Longochuk
SS0703.livelihoods: Sobat River floodplain livelihoods: maize cropping, cattle and fishing are equally important; a net cereal importer, relatively isolated near the Ethiopian border.
SS0703.history: Eastern Jikany Nuer (Gajaak) and Koma county near Ethiopia and Sudan's Blue Nile; largely pro-opposition in 2013-2018, when SPLA offensives displaced civilians.
SS0703.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that defections after 2018 led to fighting between SPLA-IO and former SPLA-IO forces in February-March 2022, and to clashes between the national army (SSPDF) and SPLA-IO in Mathiang in June 2023. ACLED records no political-violence events located in the county itself, despite this reported fighting. Armed conflict has nonetheless displaced more people here than in most counties since 2020. The vast majority of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and most still did in 2025, one of the highest levels in the country.

SS0704.name: Luakpiny/Nasir
SS0704.livelihoods: Sobat River floodplain livelihoods: maize cropping, cattle and fishing are equally important; a net cereal importer, relatively isolated near the Ethiopian border.
SS0704.history: Eastern Jikany Nuer (Gaagwang, Gaajok) county on the Sobat River around Nasir port town, a focal point of Anya-Nya 2 and later opposition activity.
SS0704.conflict_impact: Fighting between the national army (SSPDF) and the White Army began in Nasir in February 2025 and spread along the Sobat River, driving a nationwide spike in violence, according to UNMISS. ACLED records relatively high levels of political violence, with deaths at their highest in 2025. Armed conflict has displaced thousands of people since 2020, and the county has received a substantial number of people fleeing Sudan's war. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and nearly as many still did in 2025, among the highest levels in the country.

SS0705.name: Maban
SS0705.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism: sorghum and livestock, supplemented by Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade; mechanised farming near the Nile, otherwise subsistence with a cereal deficit.
SS0705.history: Mabanese (Tom, Dagu, Buni) and Burun county including Bunj; hosts large refugee camps whose population far exceeds the host population.
SS0705.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that militia violence and attacks on aid compounds in Bunj in 2018 and 2019 declined after the 2018 peace deal, while floods in late 2019 cut off access. ACLED records relatively little political violence compared with other counties, with deaths highest in 2021. Communal violence has displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020, and Maban, which already hosts large refugee camps, has become one of the main destinations for people fleeing Sudan's war. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2019 peak, and about half still did in 2025.

SS0706.name: Maiwut
SS0706.livelihoods: Sobat River floodplain livelihoods: maize cropping, cattle and fishing are equally important; a net cereal importer, relatively isolated near the Ethiopian border.
SS0706.history: Eastern Jikany Nuer (Gajaak) and Koma county on the Ethiopian border; Pagak hosted the SPLA-IO's headquarters during 2013-2018, and a 2017-18 offensive displaced tens of thousands to Ethiopia.
SS0706.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that SPLA-IO defections after 2018, notably in August 2019, sparked tensions within the Gajaak community and fighting in December 2019 and January 2020. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2018. Displacement within the county has been comparatively limited, peaking in 2020. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak; the share has since fallen considerably.

SS0707.name: Malakal
SS0707.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism: sorghum and livestock, supplemented by Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade; mechanised farming near the Nile, otherwise subsistence with a cereal deficit.
SS0707.history: Contains Malakal, Upper Nile State capital since 1914, claimed by both Shilluk and Padang Dinka; control alternated between SPLA and SPLA-IO in 2013-2018. Hosts the Malakal PoC site.
SS0707.conflict_impact: Tens of thousands of people fled to the Malakal Protection of Civilians site during the 2022 fighting in Upper Nile, and ethnic clashes took place there and at Upper Nile University in 2023, according to UNMISS. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths peaking in 2022. Malakal has one of the largest displaced populations in the country, peaking in 2024, and is one of the main destinations for people fleeing Sudan's war. Hunger has worsened recently: most residents faced crisis-level food insecurity at the 2024 peak, and nearly as many still did in 2025.

SS0708.name: Manyo
SS0708.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism: sorghum and livestock, supplemented by Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade; mechanised farming near the Nile, otherwise subsistence with a cereal deficit.
SS0708.history: Shilluk (Chollo) county in the far north of the west bank of the White Nile, with land, water and grazing disputes involving neighbouring Renk.
SS0708.conflict_impact: Fighting between Shilluk forces and Kitgwang-allied militias spread into Manyo in November and December 2022, displacing thousands, according to UNMISS. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2021. Displacement reached its highest level in early 2025, floods have displaced thousands, and the county has received a substantial number of people fleeing Sudan's war. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and more than half still did in 2025.

SS0709.name: Melut
SS0709.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism: sorghum and livestock, supplemented by Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade; mechanised farming near the Nile, otherwise subsistence with a cereal deficit.
SS0709.history: Dinka (Ageer) county on the east bank of the White Nile, containing the Melut oil basin; a strategic location in both civil wars.
SS0709.conflict_impact: CSRF describes Melut as relatively stable since 2018, and it hosted thousands of people displaced by the 2022 fighting in Upper Nile (UNMISS). ACLED records relatively little political violence, with deaths highest in 2022. Floods have displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020, and the county has received thousands of people fleeing Sudan's war. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2023 peak, and about half still did in 2025.

SS0710.name: Panyikang
SS0710.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism: sorghum and livestock, supplemented by Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade; mechanised farming near the Nile, otherwise subsistence with a cereal deficit.
SS0710.history: Shilluk (Chollo) and Padang Dinka county on the White Nile corridor south of Malakal, at the edge of the Shilluk Kingdom; heavily fought over in 2013-2018.
SS0710.conflict_impact: According to UNMISS, the August 2022 conflict in Upper Nile began with clashes between Agwelek and Kitgwang forces in Panyikang on 10 August. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths peaking in 2022. Floods and communal clashes have displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020. Hunger has been among the most severe in the country: the vast majority of residents faced crisis-level food insecurity at the 2018 peak, and most still did in 2025.

SS0711.name: Renk
SS0711.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism: sorghum and livestock, supplemented by Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade; mechanised farming near the Nile, otherwise subsistence with a cereal deficit.
SS0711.history: Dinka (Abialang) county at South Sudan's northern tip around Renk town, strategically located and contested in past civil wars; seasonal Falata herder movements have caused disputes.
SS0711.conflict_impact: Since April 2023 the Joda/Wunthow border crossing in Renk has been the main entry point for people fleeing Sudan's war, with hundreds of thousands crossing (REACH, MSF). ACLED records relatively little political violence, with deaths highest in 2023. Renk is among the counties where floods have displaced the most people since 2020, and displacement peaked in 2024. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger in 2025, the highest level recorded for the county.

SS0712.name: Ulang
SS0712.livelihoods: Sobat River floodplain livelihoods: maize cropping, cattle and fishing are equally important; a net cereal importer, relatively isolated near the Ethiopian border.
SS0712.history: Eastern Jikany Nuer (Gaajok) county on the Sobat River bordering Ethiopia and Jonglei, at the boundary between Lou and Jikany Nuer lands.
SS0712.conflict_impact: CSRF and UNMISS report fighting between Lou and Jikany Nuer near Doma in March 2019, deadly clashes within the Gaajok community in May 2021, and the impact of the 2025 hostilities between the national army (SSPDF) and the White Army. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2025. Armed conflict has displaced more people here than in almost any other county since 2020. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and most still did in 2025, among the highest levels in the country.

SS0801.name: Gogrial East

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0801.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum (staple), maize and groundnuts with cattle, goats and sheep (most households own cattle), plus fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit, trading livestock for grain.
SS0801.history: Rek Dinka (Apuk-Giir) agro-pastoral county with headquarters at Liet-Nhom; not directly hit by 2013-2018 fighting but a major recruitment area for government forces.
SS0801.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that land and boundary disputes tied to competition among local elites, along with cross-border violence with Unity State in 2019, have driven insecurity since 2018. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with civilians frequently targeted and deaths peaking in 2021. Communal violence has displaced more people here than in almost any other county since 2020, and floods have displaced tens of thousands more. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2019 peak, but conditions have since improved.

SS0802.name: Gogrial West

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0802.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum (staple), maize and groundnuts with cattle, goats and sheep (most households own cattle), plus fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit, trading livestock for grain.
SS0802.history: Rek Dinka (Aguok and Apuk) county containing Kuajok, the Warrap State capital, and Gogrial town (county HQ); a recruitment base for state forces in 2014 and 2018-19.
SS0802.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that disputes with Jur River communities over Nyinakook have caused intermittent violence, and that competition among elites has shaped local conflict since 2018. ACLED records relatively little political violence, with deaths highest in 2023. Flooding is the main driver of displacement: Gogrial West is among the counties where floods have displaced the most people since 2020, and displacement peaked in 2021. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, but the share has since fallen considerably.

SS0803.name: Tonj East

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0803.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum (staple), maize and groundnuts with cattle, goats and sheep (most households own cattle), plus fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit, trading livestock for grain.
SS0803.history: Luac-Jang and Rek Dinka county with headquarters at Romic; rich dry-season grazing lands bordering Lakes and Unity states.
SS0803.conflict_impact: A 2020 disarmament campaign around Romic ended in heavy loss of life, according to the UN Panel of Experts, and UNMISS found that armed groups from Tonj East and Tonj North caused the most civilian victims in Warrap in 2024. ACLED places Tonj East among the deadliest counties in South Sudan, with deaths peaking in 2024. Communal violence has displaced more people here than in almost any other county since 2020, and floods have displaced tens of thousands more. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2022 peak, and a large minority still did in 2025.

SS0804.name: Tonj North

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0804.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum (staple), maize and groundnuts with cattle, goats and sheep (most households own cattle), plus fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit, trading livestock for grain.
SS0804.history: Rek Dinka county with headquarters at Warrap town; Greater Tonj elites are prominent in national politics. Only limited direct effects from the 2013-2018 war.
SS0804.conflict_impact: Since 2019, violence between clans and sub-sections has surged amid recruitment linked to the 2018 peace agreement (R-ARCSS), and UNMISS found that armed elements from Tonj East and Tonj North caused most of Warrap's civilian victims in 2024. According to ACLED, Tonj North has recorded more deaths from political violence than any other county since 2018, including the most civilian deaths, with the toll peaking in 2021. Communal violence has displaced more people here than anywhere else in the country since 2020, floods have displaced tens of thousands more, and the county's displaced population is among the largest. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2022 peak; the share has since fallen considerably.

SS0805.name: Tonj South
SS0805.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum, groundnuts and other crops combined with cattle, goats and sheep; moderately productive, with acute dry-season water shortages and seasonal cattle raiding.
SS0805.history: Rek Dinka and Bongo county around Tonj town, the largest town between Rumbek and Wau; no direct civil-war fighting in 2013-2018.
SS0805.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that disputes over grazing, boundaries and cattle raiding fuelled repeated clashes in 2020, and that 2021 brought both drought and floods. ACLED records relatively high levels of political violence, with deaths peaking in 2020. Floods have displaced more people here than in most counties since 2020, and communal violence tens of thousands more, with displacement peaking in 2021. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2022 peak, but conditions have since improved considerably.

SS0806.name: Twic

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0806.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum (staple), maize and groundnuts with cattle, goats and sheep (most households own cattle), plus fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit, trading livestock for grain.
SS0806.history: Twic Mayardit Dinka county with headquarters at Turalei, bordering the Abyei Area; not directly affected by 2013-2018 fighting.
SS0806.conflict_impact: Border fighting between Twic and Ngok Dinka communities since February 2022 made Warrap the state with the most civilian victims in 2023, according to UNMISS, and there were also clashes with youth from Mayom in 2022. ACLED places Twic among the deadliest counties in the country, with deaths peaking in 2023. The county has one of the largest displaced populations in South Sudan; floods and communal violence have each displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020, with flood displacement among the highest anywhere. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2019 peak, and a large minority still did in 2025.

SS0001.name: Abyei

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0001.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum (staple), maize and groundnuts with cattle, goats and sheep (most households own cattle), plus fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit, trading livestock for grain.
SS0001.history: Abyei Administrative Area, contested between Sudan and South Sudan since 1905 boundary decisions; Ngok Dinka mainly in the south, Misseriya mainly in the north. Policed by UN force UNISFA.
SS0001.conflict_impact: Clashes at Kolom killed dozens of people in January 2020, and border violence between Twic and Ngok Dinka communities that began in February 2022 escalated again in late 2023 (CSRF, UNMISS). ACLED places Abyei among the deadliest areas in the country, with many civilians targeted and deaths peaking in 2023. Communal violence has displaced more people here than in almost any other area since 2020, floods have displaced tens of thousands, and Abyei has become one of the main destinations for people fleeing Sudan's war. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger in 2023.

SS0901.name: Jur River

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0901.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum (staple), maize and groundnuts with cattle, goats and sheep (most households own cattle), plus fishing and wild foods; cereal deficit, trading livestock for grain. Also partly in the Ironstone Plateau agro-pastoral and Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum zones.
SS0901.history: Home to Balanda Bor, Luo ('Jur Chol') and Dinka Marial Bai communities, headquarters Nyin Akok; the 2014 Mapel training-centre clash occurred here. Little direct impact from the 2013-18 war.
SS0901.conflict_impact: Tens of thousands of people fled communal clashes between February and June 2019, especially in Kuarjena and Rocrocdong payams (IOM displacement tracking, via CSRF), and disputes between Luo and Dinka Marial Bai communities persist (UNMISS). ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with civilians frequently targeted and deaths peaking in 2019. Communal violence and floods have each displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2019 peak, but food security has improved markedly since.

SS0902.name: Raja

livelihood_zone.name: Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum

SS0902.livelihoods: Subsistence rain-fed farming of groundnuts, sesame and sorghum, supplemented by forest products, seasonal river fishing and sales of poultry, goats and sheep; a former surplus area.
SS0902.history: Largest county, bordering Sudan and CAR, home to many 'Fertit' groups (Kresh, Balanda, Banda, Aja and others) around Raja town. SPLA-IO briefly overran Raja town in June 2016.
SS0902.conflict_impact: Forces of Paul Malong's South Sudan United Front/Army (SSUF/A) were defeated in Raja in August 2019, according to CSRF, and since 2023 tensions have grown around gold mining at Boro Medina while the road north to South Darfur remains insecure. ACLED records relatively little political violence in Raja compared with other counties, with deaths highest in 2018. Displacement within the county has been modest, peaking in 2019, though floods have forced thousands from their homes and Raja has become one of the main destinations for people fleeing Sudan's war since 2023. Hunger was severe at its 2018 peak, when most residents faced crisis-level food insecurity or worse, and has since eased, though a significant minority still face crisis conditions.

SS0903.name: Wau

livelihood_zone.name: Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum

SS0903.livelihoods: Subsistence rain-fed farming of groundnuts, sesame and sorghum, supplemented by forest products, seasonal river fishing and sales of poultry, goats and sheep; a former surplus area.
SS0903.history: Contains Wau, capital of Western Bahr el Ghazal, with Balanda and other 'Fertit', Luo ('Jur Chol') and Dinka communities; June 2016 attacks in Wau town drove mass displacement to the UN PoC site.
SS0903.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that fighting between government and opposition forces around Mboro and Baggari in 2018 eased in 2019, but SPLA-IO defections and splits keep the Baggari area insecure. ACLED records moderate levels of political violence, with deaths highest in 2018. Wau has hosted one of the largest displaced populations in the country, peaking in 2019, and has become one of the main destinations for people fleeing Sudan's war. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, but food security has improved markedly since.

SS1001.name: Ezo

secondary.name: Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum

SS1001.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the bimodal-rainfall Greenbelt, normally a surplus area: maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava, beans; supplemented by small livestock, fishing, hunting and wild/bush products, with cross-border trade. Also partly in the Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum zone.
SS1001.history: Zande (Azande) county with headquarters at Ezo town, bordering DR Congo and CAR; long exposed to LRA attacks and cross-border armed groups.
SS1001.conflict_impact: Tens of thousands of people fled the 2021 violence in Tambura into Ezo, and UNMISS reported that hundreds of Ezo youths were recruited and sent to Tambura in September 2021 (CSRF). ACLED records relatively little political violence within the county, with deaths highest in 2025. Communal and armed conflict have displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020, and displacement peaked in 2022. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, but the county now has among the lowest levels of food insecurity in the country.

SS1002.name: Ibba
SS1002.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the bimodal-rainfall Greenbelt, normally a surplus area: maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava, beans; supplemented by small livestock, fishing, hunting and wild/bush products, with cross-border trade.
SS1002.history: Azande, Baka and Mundu county with headquarters at Ibba town; hit by LRA abductions from 2005-06.
SS1002.conflict_impact: Clashes between residents and Mbororo-Fulani herders rose from 2022, and a deadly attack in spring 2023 displaced thousands of people (UN Security Council, via CSRF). ACLED records very little political violence compared with other counties. Displacement has otherwise been limited. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, but the county now has among the lowest levels of food insecurity in the country.

SS1003.name: Maridi
SS1003.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the bimodal-rainfall Greenbelt, normally a surplus area: maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava, beans; supplemented by small livestock, fishing, hunting and wild/bush products, with cross-border trade.
SS1003.history: Baka, Mundu, Avukaya, Zande and Moro Kodo county with headquarters at Maridi town; land disputes date to land given to SPLA soldiers in the 1990s.
SS1003.conflict_impact: CSRF reports persistent tensions between farmers and pastoralists over crop damage and contested land, and clashes between SPLA-IO and government forces in 2016-17. ACLED records relatively little political violence since 2018, with deaths highest in 2021. Displacement has been comparatively limited. Food insecurity has been among the lowest in the country throughout the period.

SS1004.name: Mundri East
SS1004.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the bimodal-rainfall Greenbelt, normally a surplus area: maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava, beans; supplemented by small livestock, fishing, hunting and wild/bush products, with cross-border trade. Also partly in the Ironstone Plateau agro-pastoral zone.
SS1004.history: Moru and Mundu county with headquarters at Kediba, on the Western-Central Equatoria border; dry-season herds from Lakes and Central Equatoria migrate here.
SS1004.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported operations by the national army (SSPDF) against the National Salvation Front (NAS), and abuses by NAS, that affected civilians in Mundri East in 2024. ACLED records relatively little political violence overall, but deaths rose to their highest level in 2025. Armed conflict has displaced more people here than in almost any other county since 2020, and communal clashes have displaced thousands more. About half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and food insecurity is now relatively low.

SS1005.name: Mundri West
SS1005.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the bimodal-rainfall Greenbelt, normally a surplus area: maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava, beans; supplemented by small livestock, fishing, hunting and wild/bush products, with cross-border trade.
SS1005.history: Moru, Belle and Mundu county with headquarters at Mundri town; greater Mundri has seen growing farmer-herder polarisation since 2005.
SS1005.conflict_impact: UNMISS attributed many of the abductions in the Mundri area in 2020 mainly to the National Salvation Front (NAS). ACLED records relatively little political violence compared with other counties, with deaths highest in 2023. Displacement has been among the lowest in the country, though armed conflict and floods have each displaced thousands since 2020. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and food insecurity is now relatively low.

SS1006.name: Mvolo
SS1006.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral: sorghum, groundnuts and other crops combined with cattle, goats and sheep; moderately productive, with acute dry-season water shortages and seasonal cattle raiding.
SS1006.history: Belle ('Jur Bel'), Bongo, Wira, Nyamusa and Moru county with headquarters at Mvolo town, closely linked to Wulu (Lakes); hosted the Mvolo peace conference.
SS1006.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that security improved after the 2018 peace agreement (R-ARCSS), but violence by often unidentified groups rose again during 2020. ACLED records relatively little political violence, with deaths highest that year. Displacement has been among the lowest in the country, though floods and communal clashes have each displaced thousands since 2020. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak; the share has since fallen considerably.

SS1007.name: Nagero

livelihood_zone.name: Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum

SS1007.livelihoods: Subsistence rain-fed farming of groundnuts, sesame and sorghum, supplemented by forest products, seasonal river fishing and sales of poultry, goats and sheep; a former surplus area.
SS1007.history: Remote Balanda, Bongo and Azande county with headquarters at Nagero town; SPLA-IO briefly seized Nagero in May 2018, followed by an SPLA counter-offensive.
SS1007.conflict_impact: Nagero hosted thousands of mainly Balanda people displaced by the 2021 violence in Tambura, and CSRF found that displaced people made up most of those in need. ACLED records relatively little political violence within the county, with deaths highest in 2025. Communal violence has displaced tens of thousands of people since 2020, and displacement reached its highest level in early 2025. Most residents faced crisis-level hunger at the 2018 peak, and a large minority still did in 2025.

SS1008.name: Nzara

secondary.name: Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum

SS1008.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the bimodal-rainfall Greenbelt, normally a surplus area: maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava, beans; supplemented by small livestock, fishing, hunting and wild/bush products, with cross-border trade. Also partly in the Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum zone.
SS1008.history: Zande county with headquarters at Nzara town, site of the July 1955 Nzara demonstrations within the colonial Zande Scheme; conflict spread was limited in 2013-2018.
SS1008.conflict_impact: CSRF reports periodic low-level insecurity since 2018, such as a June 2019 incident involving the national army (SSPDF) at Mogoroko and killings in Sakure payam in September 2021. ACLED records no political-violence events located in the county over the period. Displacement has been comparatively limited. Nzara has had the lowest levels of food insecurity of any county, and few residents face crisis-level hunger today.

SS1009.name: Tambura

livelihood_zone.name: Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum

SS1009.livelihoods: Subsistence rain-fed farming of groundnuts, sesame and sorghum, supplemented by forest products, seasonal river fishing and sales of poultry, goats and sheep; a former surplus area.
SS1009.history: Azande and Balanda county with headquarters at Tambura town, bordering CAR; part of the former Tambura State.
SS1009.conflict_impact: Violence between Azande and Balanda communities from June 2021 displaced tens of thousands of people (CSRF), and renewed tensions in June 2024 led to many cases of sexual violence (UNMISS). ACLED records relatively high levels of political violence, with civilians frequently targeted and deaths peaking in 2021. The county's displaced population was among the larger in the country, peaking in 2022, with communal violence the main cause. Hunger was among the most severe in the country at its 2022 peak, affecting the vast majority of residents, but has since eased considerably.

SS1010.name: Yambio
SS1010.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the bimodal-rainfall Greenbelt, normally a surplus area: maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava, beans; supplemented by small livestock, fishing, hunting and wild/bush products, with cross-border trade.
SS1010.history: Zande county containing Yambio, capital of Western Equatoria and historic seat of the Azande Kingdom, re-established with a coronation in Feb 2022; hosts refugees from DR Congo and CAR.
SS1010.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that clashes declined after 2018, but 2021 saw targeted attacks on officials and confrontations between the national army (SSPDF) and SPLA-IO in Yambio town. ACLED records relatively little political violence, with deaths highest in 2025. Displacement peaked in 2018 and has been moderate. Food insecurity has been among the lowest in the country, and few residents face crisis-level hunger today.
